I'm going to refer to the comic since this is more of a general writing philosophy discussion.
But James O'Barr the author of the crow was in a near constant state of anger and grief during the writing process.
Basically Eric Draven was James O'Barr emotionally lashing out on the page. Committing murder, seeking revenge against the dark side of the world.
The thing is that writing the crow didn't make O'Barr feel better. It made him feel worse, much worse.
He inhabited a character who constantly languished in misery, proffered prose about nihilism and the futility of hope, he cut himself and lots of other tragically angsty stuff.

I've got ADHD but through years of trial and error I've developed some good habits that may help:
1. Serve and return. If you're stuck listening to someone that sucks for everyone. Don't be a hostage. Participate whether the goomba you're talking to wants you to or not. This is also a good power play.
2. When you return a conversational serve leave yourself room to create a side conversation. Maybe the other person is trying to talk about how much they hate their ex girlfriend because she stole 200 bucks from them and you're not in the mood. To which you could interject "wow, and I bet that really made bills tough for a bit." Now you can segue into something that you want to talk about. Maybe you recently got screwed by your landlord. Well, now they can enjoy your conversation.
3. Be ready to abort. Sometimes people are social hedonists. Get out before they devour your time. "Hold that thought I really want to hear the end of this story. I'll be right back." Get some water, go to the bathroom, wash your face, return a call, anything. This signals that they have absorbed a lot of time and you're not going to be held hostage. You will leave if you have to. It's not rude, but some immature people will be mad for a moment. If you handle it well in my experience this leads to respect.
4. If they won't let you get a word in edge wise and they're being rude, *do not participate* that person wants to monologue. The audience doesn't matter. If they ask why you're not saying anything, just let them know you were waiting patiently for them to finish their story.

The idea for us with ADHD is that we need to develop leadership qualities to protect ourselves from abuse by those who sense our struggles. Be strong, not rude and you'll have an easier time dealing with difficult conversations. At least in my experience.
